What moves the price on a B4204T41 replacement is whether the PCV system, timing belt, tensioner, water pump and turbocharger have been addressed on the donor unit. failures.title: Volvo B4204T41 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: PCV System Clogging - all VEA T5 variants including B4204T41
items.whatHappens: Crankcase ventilation (PCV) system becomes clogged with sludge and carbon deposits, increasing crankcase pressure and forcing oil past piston rings and turbo seals. Symptoms include increased oil consumption (some owners report 1 litre per 1,000 km), blue smoke from the exhaust, and possible oil leaks from seals. The higher-output T41 tune means the turbo works harder, making oil supply and PCV function even more critical.
items.repairVsReplace: PCV system cleaning or replacement (typically £300-£600) resolves the issue if caught early. If oil consumption has been ignored, the turbocharger may be damaged and require replacement (£900-£1,800). In advanced cases with piston ring gumming, a full rebuild or replacement is the only definitive fix. Read our full oil consumption guide

items.title: Timing Belt - interference engine, critical interval
items.whatHappens: The B4204T41 uses a timing belt, not a chain. As an interference engine, a failed belt or tensioner causes pistons to strike valves, destroying the cylinder head and often the bottom end. The interval is typically 90,000 miles or 10 years, but many specialists recommend earlier replacement (80,000 miles) due to reports of belt and tensioner wear on VEA petrol engines - particularly on higher-output variants where the engine works harder.
items.repairVsReplace: Belt failure is catastrophic - full engine replacement is almost always required. Preventative belt replacement at the correct interval is essential; many specialists recommend replacing the water pump, tensioner and VVT pulleys simultaneously. Read our full timing belt failure guide

items.title: Turbocharger Wear - higher-output variant, more stress
items.whatHappens: The B4204T41's higher-output calibration (around 250hp) places more stress on the turbocharger than lower-output T5 variants. The twin-scroll turbo can suffer from shaft wear, wastegate rattle, or oil seal failure, particularly if oil changes have been neglected. Symptoms include loss of power, whistling noises, blue smoke on startup, and engine management lights.
items.repairVsReplace: Turbo refurbishment (£500-£1,000) can restore function if the damage is limited to bearings and seals. Replacement with a new or reconditioned unit (£900-£1,800) is required for more serious shaft or turbine damage. Regular oil changes with the correct 0W‑20 VCC RBS0‑2AE spec are essential to protect the turbo.

failures.goodYearsLine: The B4204T41 (2014+) is a well‑developed VEA T5 calibration with improved PCV and timing components over early VEA units. However, the higher-output tune means regular maintenance - particularly oil changes and timing belt adherence - is even more critical than on lower-output variants. Cars with full service history and documented PCV/turbo care are significantly more reliable than neglected examples.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the B4204T41
variants.intro: The B4204T41 is a specific sub‑code within the VEA 2.0‑litre T5 family, introduced around 2014 as a high-output calibration. It sits between the B4204T11 (245hp) and the later B4204T23 (254hp) in the VEA timeline. Here's how it compares to other common VEA T5 codes: - B4204T11 - 245hp, 2014‑2016, earlier VEA T5, the baseline T5 tune - B4204T20 - 249hp AWD, 2015‑2018, AWD-specific calibration - B4204T41 - approx. 245‑250hp, 2014‑present, high-output FWD/AWD T5 calibration - B4204T37 - 245‑254hp, 2016‑present, later FWD T5 calibration with revised emissions - B4204T23 - 254hp, 2017‑2020, the most powerful single-turbo VEA T5 - B4204T27 - 320hp T6 twin‑charged (supercharger + turbo) - completely different configuration Where the code is found: The B4204T41 sub‑code is printed on a sticker on the timing belt cover and on the V5C registration document under "Engine number". The first three characters (B42) indicate the VEA petrol family, and the final digits give the specific variant. Commonly confused codes: The B4204T41 is often mistaken for the B4204T11 or B4204T37, but they are not identical - they have different ECU calibrations and sometimes different turbo and injector part numbers. Fitting the wrong variant can result in incorrect fuelling and limp mode. Always match the exact sub‑code when buying a replacement.

relatives.description: B4204T11 (2.0L T5, 245hp, 2014-2016): The earlier VEA T5 calibration that preceded the B4204T41. The T11 produced 245hp and was the baseline T5 from 2014-2016; the B4204T41 was the higher - output calibration with revised turbo and ECU mapping. Both are VEA architecture, but the T41 has different software, injector part numbers and a more aggressive turbo calibration - not a straight swap without matching ECU and injectors.

B4204T23 (2.0L T5, 254hp, 2017-2020): The later VEA T5 calibration that followed the B4204T41, producing 254hp with further emissions refinements and improved low - end torque. The T23 is the most powerful single-turbo T5 and is considered the pinnacle of the VEA petrol range. If you're replacing a B4204T41, the T23 is a potential upgrade but requires ECU matching and potentially different injectors and turbo part numbers.

B4204T37 (2.0L T5, updated calibration): A later FWD T5 calibration (2016+) that sits alongside the T41 in the VEA timeline. The T37 and T41 are similar in output but differ in ECU calibration and emissions compliance. Not a straight swap - check compatibility carefully.

B4204T27 (2.0L T6, 320hp twin - charged): The high-performance T6 variant of the VEA family - supercharged and turbocharged, producing 320hp. Shares the same block but has a supercharger, different ancillaries, and a completely different induction system. Not interchangeable with the T5; if you're looking for T6, you're on the wrong page.

D4204T (2.0L D4 diesel): The diesel counterpart in the VEA family - shares the same block architecture but is fundamentally different in fuelling, compression, turbo and ancillaries. If your car is diesel, you're on the wrong page.

B4204T44 / T46 (T5 PHEV hybrid variants): The hybrid versions of the VEA T5 - petrol engine combined with an electric motor. They share the block but include additional hybrid components and a different starter-generator; not a direct swap with non-hybrid T5 units.

relatives.code: The B4204T41 is a Volvo-only VEA engine, not shared with any other manufacturer. It is not related to the Ford 2.0 EcoBoost, despite both being 2.0‑litre turbos; the VEA architecture is Volvo's own design and shares no parts with Ford.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement B4204T41 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: ** A used B4204T41 can make sense for older S60, V60 or XC60 examples where the car's value is under £5,000. **Crucially:** only buy a used unit with documented PCV service history, timing belt replacement record, turbo health check, and proof of regular oil changes with the correct 0W‑20 VCC spec. A used engine without these risks inheriting the same PCV, timing and turbo issues - which could cost you the equivalent of a reconditioned unit in repairs. The higher-output T41 makes turbo condition particularly important. Used engines service

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: ** A proper B4204T41 recon addresses the PCV system, timing belt, tensioner, water pump, VVT pulleys, turbocharger inspection or refurbishment, injector seals and a full oil system flush - exactly the maintenance items that keep these engines running well into high mileage. This is the right call for any car worth over £6,000 where you plan to keep it for 2+ years. Most recon units come with a 12‑month warranty and have had all the common issues proactively fixed. Reconditioned engines service

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: ** A full B4204T41 rebuild is rarely cost‑effective compared to a reconditioned exchange unit - the labour to strip, inspect and rebuild a VEA petrol with new pistons, rings, bearings and cylinder head overhaul typically exceeds £4,500 before parts. Only consider a rebuild for a low‑mileage, high‑spec car (e.g. an XC90 T5 Inscription or a V90 T5) where the chassis is immaculate and you have a Volvo specialist who knows the VEA platform intimately. Rebuilt engines service

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: ** All replacement engines through our network are supplied with 12‑month warranty and can be fitted by Volvo specialists nationwide. Supply & fit service
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: ** The B4204T41 sits across a value range - from £4,500 S60 T5s to £28,000 XC90 T5s. For a sub‑£5,500 car, a reconditioned engine at £3,500-£4,800 may represent 70‑100% of the car's value - evaluate scrap value before committing. For XC60, XC90, S90 and V90 owners, the car's retained value comfortably absorbs a recon engine cost. Be honest about the car's condition, mileage and MOT history before deciding.

items.question: What is the common failure on the B4204T41 engine?
items.answer: The most common issues are PCV system clogging (leading to increased oil consumption), timing belt wear on an interference engine, and turbocharger wear due to the higher-output calibration - all of which can lead to catastrophic engine damage if ignored. The B4204T41 is a well-developed VEA variant with improved components over early units, but the PCV system still requires attention at higher mileages, the timing belt must be replaced at the recommended interval (90,000 miles or 8‑10 years), and the turbo benefits from regular oil changes with the correct 0W‑20 VCC RBS0‑2AE spec. PCV clogging: oil consumption can exceed 1L per 1,000km. Timing belt interval: 90,000 miles or 8‑10 years - failure = full engine replacement. Turbo wear: higher-output tune means more stress - regular oil changes essential.

items.answer: It depends on your car's value and the service history of the donor engine. For an older S60 or V60 valued under £5,000, a used unit with documented PCV, timing belt and turbo history (£2,200-£3,500) may be the only financially sensible option. items.question: What's the difference between B4204T11, B4204T41, B4204T37 and B4204T23?
items.answer: These are all VEA 2.0‑litre T5 petrol variants with different calibrations and production years. B4204T11 is 245hp (2014‑2016) - the baseline T5. B4204T41 is the high-output calibration (245‑250hp, 2014‑present) with a more aggressive turbo tune. B4204T37 is a later FWD calibration (245‑254hp, 2016‑present) with revised emissions. B4204T23 is the most powerful single-turbo T5 (254hp, 2017‑2020) with the latest refinements. They share the same block but differ in ECU software, injectors, and sometimes turbo part numbers. They are not directly interchangeable without matching the ECU and ancillaries. B4204T11: 245hp, 2014‑2016, baseline T5. B4204T41: 245‑250hp, 2014‑present, high-output calibration. B4204T37: 245‑254hp, 2016‑present, revised FWD calibration. B4204T23: 254hp, 2017‑2020, most powerful single-turbo T5.

items.question: How long does a B4204T41 engine last?
items.answer: With proper maintenance - especially strict adherence to the timing belt interval, regular oil changes with the correct 0W‑20 VCC spec, and PCV system service - 150,000-200,000 miles is achievable before major work is needed. The key factors are: (1) timing belt replacement at 90,000 miles or 8‑10 years - failure is catastrophic; (2) PCV system cleaning or replacement around 80,000-100,000 miles to prevent oil consumption; (3) oil changes at 10,000 miles or annually with the correct spec - the higher-output T41 makes turbo health particularly dependent on clean oil. Many VEA T5 units exceed 200,000 miles with these items addressed proactively. Timing belt is the single most important service item. PCV issues typically emerge between 80,000-120,000 miles. Turbo health depends on regular oil changes - use only the recommended 0W‑20 oil.
